claim: RORγ is an orphan nuclear receptor that is widely expressed and is involved in regulation of various metabolic processes.
source: RAR-Related Orphan Receptor C (RORγ, gene name RORC) is an orphan nuclear receptor (NR) that is widely expressed and is involved in regulation of various metabolic processes (Bookout et al., 2006; Takeda et al., 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to published literature (Bookout et al., 2006; Takeda et al., 2012).

claim: RORγt is a master regulator of the IL-17 producing T helper (Th17) cell subset.
source: RORγ is also a key player in the immune system where the lymphocyte specific isoform RORγt is a so-called 'master regulator' of the IL-17 producing T helper (Th17) cell subset (Ivanov et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Ivanov et al., 2006.

claim: Human patients with nonsense mutations in RORγ are susceptible to candida infection of the lung.
source: Human patients with nonsense mutations are susceptible to candida infection of the lung (Okada et al., 2015), suggesting that the evolutionary pressure of RORγ weighs heavily on immune function.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Okada et al., 2015.

claim: RORγ is the driver of the androgen receptor in metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer.
source: More recently, RORγ has also been found to be the driver of the androgen receptor in metastatic castration resistant prostate cancer where the selective RORγ antagonist SR2211 elicits a potent cytostatic effect (Wang et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wang et al., 2016.

claim: Synthetic RORγ agonists hyperactivate the receptor beyond the level achieved by endogenous ligands.
source: While activating ligands of RORγt are present during T cell maturation (Hu et al., 2015), synthetic RORγ agonists have been found to further activate the receptor (hyperactivation) (Chang et al., 2016; Marcotte et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2015; Chang et al., 2016; Marcotte et al., 2016.

claim: RORγ agonists increase IL-17 expression and decrease PD-1 levels.
source: Interestingly, our lab and others have demonstrated that RORγ agonists not only increase expression of IL-17 expression, but also decrease levels of programmed cell death one receptor (PD-1) (Chang et al., 2016; Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Chang et al., 2016 and Hu et al., 2016.

claim: Chimeric antigen receptor expressing T cells treated with RORγ agonists potentiate tumor clearance activity in mouse models.
source: Indeed, chimeric antigen receptor expressing T cells treated with RORγ agonists potentiate tumor clearance activity in mouse models (Hu et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hu et al., 2016.

claim: The RORγ ligand binding domain is comprised of 12 α-helices (H1-H12) and a β-sheet region (BSR).
source: Structural and functional analysis has revealed that the RORγ ligand binding domain (RORγLBD) is comprised of 12 α-helices (H1-H12) and a β-sheet region (BSR) that responds to cholesterol biosynthetic pathway intermediates, hydroxysterols and sterol sulfates (Hu et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2010; Santori et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hu et al., 2015; Jin et al., 2010; Santori et al., 2015.

claim: The gauche rotomeric state of W317 stabilizes H11, H11' and H12 through extensive hydrophobic interaction networks.
source: Collectively, these studies have identified that the gauche rotomeric state of W317 stabilizes H11, H11' and H12 through extensive hydrophobic interaction networks formed with F486, F506, Y502, and H479 as the key drivers of RORγ hyperactivation by stabilizing the required Y502-H479 hydrogen bond.
evidence: The claim is based on inference from previous studies mentioned in the text (Li et al., 2017; Sun et al., 2018; Yukawa et al., 2019).

claim: In-line pepsin digestion of RORγLBD and LC-MS analysis reliably yields 54 peptides that cover 98% of the primary sequence.
source: In-line pepsin digestion of RORγLBD and LC-MS analysis reliably yields 54 peptides that cover 98% of the primary sequence, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from HDX-MS analysis and reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H10-H12 of RORγLBD exhibits fast kinetics or little protection to solvent exchange.
source: During a 10 s to 4 hr time course, the majority of the sequence exhibits intermediate to slow kinetics, or moderate protection to exchange (Figure 2C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D–1E), while H10-H12 exhibits fast kinetics, or little protection to solvent exchange, Figure 2D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS experimental data shown in the referenced figures.

claim: In the presence of 25-hydroxycholesterol or SR19265, several regions of RORγ became protected to solvent exchange with the most dramatic being the BSR and H12.
source: In the presence of endogenous ligands or partial agonists, such as 25-hydroxycholesterol (25OHC) or SR19265, several regions of RORγ became protected to solvent exchange with the most dramatic being the BSR and H12 (Figure 1F and G).
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS experimental data shown in Figure 1F and G.

claim: RORγLBD bound to SR2211 exhibited protection to amides surrounding the orthosteric binding site, but SR2211 offered no protection to H12.
source: HDX-MS analysis of the selective RORγ inverse agonist SR2211 revealed a distinctive profile. Specifically, RORγLBD bound to SR2211 exhibited protection to amides surrounding the orthosteric binding site, but SR2211 offered no protection to H12 suggesting that the activation function surface remains disordered.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: The co-crystal structure solution of the RORγLBD bound to SR2211 reveals a deactivation where the carbinol moiety pushes W317 into an alternative conformation that prevent H11' and H12 from nucleating.
source: The co-crystal structure solution of the RORγLBD bound to SR2211 reveals a deactivation where the carbinol moiety pushes W317 into an alternative conformation that prevent H11' and H12 from nucleating.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: The presence of SRC1-2 resulted in further protection to H4 and H10-12 consistent with ternary complex formation.
source: The presence of SRC1-2 resulted in further protection to H4 and H10-12 consistent with published co-crystal structure solutions with coactivator peptides indicating ternary complex formation (Jin et al., 2010), Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data and corroborated by citation to Jin et al., 2010.

claim: The RORγLBD-SRC2 fusion construct demonstrated similar kinetics to the ternary complex suggesting that the fusion construct artificially stabilizes the active conformer in solution.
source: We also compared the dynamics of the RORγLBD-SRC2 fusion construct (RORγ265–507-GGG-SRC2-2), which was used to solve the 'apo' RORγ crystal structure, with our RORγLBD construct. This construct demonstrated similar kinetics of the ternary complex suggesting that the fusion construct artificially stabilizes the active conformer in solution, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and E.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS experimental data comparing the fusion construct with the ternary complex.

claim: SR19265 was able to interact with SRC1-2 peptide with similar potency and fold activation of the reported endogenous agonists 25OHC and desmosterol.
source: SR19265 was able to interact with a synthetic peptide derived from SRC1 NR-box 2 (SRC1-2) with similar potency and fold activation of the reported endogenous agonists 25OHC and desmosterol, Figure 1B.
evidence: The claim is supported by AlphaScreen-based coactivator peptide interaction assay data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: SR19265 exhibited a marked reduction in potency in cell-based assays compared to biochemical assays.
source: However, SR19265 exhibited a marked reduction in potency and the differences in activity were non-significantly different from the DMSO treated control group at a 1 µM dose compared to biochemical assays, Figure 1E.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of biochemical and cell-based assay data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: SR19265 binding is located further away from R367 and the interaction is driven strictly through hydrophobic contacts.
source: While 3-hydroxy and 3-sulfocholesterols are thought to be stabilized by hydrophobic contacts and hydrogen bonds with R367 (Jin et al., 2010; Kallen et al., 2017). SR19265 binding was located further away from R367 and the interaction is driven strictly through hydrophobic contacts.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data and comparison with published structures.

claim: SR19265 makes hydrophobic contacts with W317 and H479 thereby stabilizing H10 and H12 through the W317-F486 π stacking and H479-Y502 hydrogen bond respectively.
source: SR19265 makes hydrophobic contacts with W317 and H479 thereby stabilizing H10 and H12 through the W317-F486 π stacking and H479-Y502 hydrogen bond respectively, Figure 2A.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: A368V mutation selectively disrupts hydroxycholesterol binding but not SR19265 binding.
source: We hypothesized that a simple mutation to A368 could selectively disrupt hydroxycholesterol binding but not SR19265 binding. Using the SRC1-2 coactivator peptide interaction assay, we observed a marked reduction in hydroxycholesterol-mediated activation of A368V RORγLBD while SR19265 retained potency compared to the WT variant.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from coactivator peptide interaction assays.

claim: The A368V mutation is a loss of function where activity is recoverable with synthetic modulator SR19265.
source: In the cell-based promotor reporter assay, the A368V mutation is a loss of function where activity is recoverable with synthetic modulator, Figure 1D.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-based promoter reporter assay data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: A368V RORγLBD treated with SR19265 showed similar protection to exchange as the WT RORγLBD treated with SR19265.
source: On the other hand, A368V RORγLBD treated with SR19265, Figure 1H, showed similar protection to exchange as the WT RORγLBD treated with SR19265, Figure 1F, suggesting that the A368V variant liganded with SR19265 maintained similar structural dynamics to the WT receptor bound to SR19265.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data comparing WT and A368V variants shown in Figures 1F and 1H.

claim: SR19547 treatment enhances the EC50 of RORγLBD association with SRC1-2 to 1 μM compared to 53 μM for the DMSO treated protein control.
source: In a fluorescence polarization-based coactivator peptide interaction assay, SR19265 and SR19547 treatment enhances the EC50 of RORγLBD association with SRC1-2 to 12 μM and 1 μM respectively compared to 53 μM for the DMSO treated protein control, Figure 2E.
evidence: The claim is supported by fluorescence polarization assay data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SR19547 is able to hyperactivate RORγ about 50–80% above the basal level in cell-based assays.
source: The enhanced affinity for coactivator is consistent with the cell-based assays results where SR19547 is able to hyperactivate RORγ about 50–80% above the basal level, Figure 2F.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-based assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The amide of SR19355 acts as a H-bond donor for H479, which disrupts the H479-Y502 H-bond leading to destabilization of H12.
source: Interestingly, the amide of SR19355 acts as a H-bond donor for H479, which disrupts the H479-Y502 H-bond leading to destabilization of H12.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: SR19265 treatment protects H12 to solvent exchange, whereas SR19355 treatment does not protect H12.
source: This finding is corroborated by HDX-MS where SR19265 treatment protects H12, whereas SR19355 treatment does not protect H12 to solvent exchange.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS experimental data.

claim: SR19547 treatment results in protection to H3, the BSR, with stronger protection to H12, indicating that SR19547 strongly stabilizes the active conformation of RORγ.
source: Despite this, we were still able to study the effects of SR19547 on the dynamics of the RORγLBD where we see protection to H3, the BSR, with stronger protection to H12, Figure 2C and D, indicating that SR19547 strongly stabilizes the active conformation of RORγ.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 2C and 2D.

claim: All compounds generally engaged the receptor in the orthosteric ligand binding pocket based on observed protection to H3-H7 and the BSR.
source: All compounds were found to generally engage the receptor in the orthosteric ligand binding pocket based on observed protection to H3-H7 and the BSR.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS screening data of 38 compounds.

claim: H12 stability at the 10 s timepoint correlated (R2 = 0.638) with the ligand-dependent recruitment of SRC1-2.
source: As expected, we observed that H12 stability at the 10 s timepoint correlated (R2 = 0.638) with the ligand-dependent recruitment of SRC1-2, Figure 3E.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of HDX-MS and functional assay data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: Perturbation values of H4 at the 4 hr timepoint correlated (R2 = 0.476) with coactivator recruitment activity.
source: We also observed that perturbation values of H4 at the 4 hr timepoint correlated (R2 = 0.476) with coactivator recruitment activity, Figure 3B.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of HDX-MS and functional assay data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Protection to the BSR showed somewhat predictive correlation (R2 = 0.538) with thermal stability.
source: While perturbation values of peptides from four regions (H2, H3, the BSR, and H7), Figure 3G, were found to have with significantly nonzero correlation coefficients in a linear model, only protection to the BSR showed somewhat predictive correlation (R2 = 0.538), Figure 3H.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of HDX-MS and thermal shift assay data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: Activity in cell-based assays was best predicted by protection to H2 (R2 = 0.512) and H7 (R2 = 0.496).
source: Interestingly, protection to H12 became a less significant predictor (R2 = 0.392) of activity within cells, Figure 3F. Instead, activity in cell-based assays was best predicted by protection to H2 (R2 = 0.512) and H7 (R2 = 0.496), Figure 3C and I.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of HDX-MS and cell-based assay data shown in Figures 3C and 3I.

claim: Ligand-dependent perturbation values clustered into three groups: H12 with H1, H4 and H10; the BSR with H3 and H7; and a single peptide from H2.
source: We found that ligand-dependent perturbation values clustered into three groups, Figure 4B. The first group correlated with H12 and consisted of H1, H4 and H10. While most compounds protected H12, SR19269 and SR19355 exhibited little protection to this region. This helped to determine whether the correlations were coincidental, or dependent on H12 stability. Since SR19355 and SR19269 were clear outliers in the H12-H1 correlation plot, Figure 4D, this correlation was likely coincidental where H1 happens to be more stable when H12 is stable. However, SR19355 and SR19269 also exhibit commensurate H4 protection showing that the observed H4 stability depends on H12 stability. Furthermore, a correlation coefficient of 0.779 suggests that a simple linear model explains most of the variance of the distribution, Figure 4C. The second cluster were correlated strongly (R2 >0.7) with the BSR and consisted of H3 and H7. SR19269 and SR19355 did not appear to be obvious outliers with the second group. This region is likely where compounds were directly engaging the protein, so it is unclear that the stabilities of the region depended on each other or were simply driven by varying degrees of ligand binding. The third group consisted of a single peptide from H2, shown in green in Figure 4B, which correlated with both H12 and the BSR.
evidence: The claim is supported by covariation analysis of HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: H4 stability depends on H12 stability.
source: However, SR19355 and SR19269 also exhibit commensurate H4 protection showing that the observed H4 stability depends on H12 stability.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing that compounds that do not stabilize H12 also do not stabilize H4.

claim: K354A and K503A are loss of function mutations in cell-based assays.
source: Introducing either K503A or K354A variations to a GAL4-RORγLBD resulted in a loss of function in cell-based assays, Figure 5B.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-based assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Mutation to K503R, but not K354R, was able to retain activity similar to WT levels.
source: Mutation to K503R, but not K354R, was able to retain activity similar to WT levels, indicating general electrostatic interactions at K503 but not K354 are sufficient for activation.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-based assay data.

claim: Treatment with synthetic agonist SR19547 was able to recover activity of the K503A construct, but not the K354A mutant.
source: Treatment with synthetic agonist SR19547 was able to recover activity of the K503A construct, but not the K354A mutant suggesting the H12-H4 interaction is essential to activate RORγ in situ.
evidence: The claim is supported by cell-based assay data.

claim: Protection to H10-12 was disrupted in varying degrees between the K354A and K503A variant receptors with K354A being the most severe.
source: Strikingly, protection to H10-12 was disrupted in varying degrees between the variant receptors with K354A being the most severe, Figure 5E and H.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figures 5E and 5H.

claim: At the 10 s timepoint, H12 of K354A RORγLBD is completely deuterated, much like apo WT RORγLBD.
source: At the 10 s timepoint, H12 of K354A RORγLBD is completely deuterated, Figure 5H, much like apo WT RORγLBD.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The K354A variant exhibits faster kinetics at H4 consistent with previous findings in the covariance study.
source: Furthermore, the K354A variant exhibits faster kinetics at H4 consistent with previous findings in the covariance study.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data and is consistent with earlier covariance analysis.

claim: Ligand-dependent conformational changes assessed with HDX-MS can empirically correlate with functional assay activity to reveal structural determinants for various biochemical activities.
source: Here we demonstrate that ligand-dependent conformational changes, assessed with HDX-MS, can empirically correlate with functional assay activity to reveal structural determinants for various biochemical activities.
evidence: The claim is supported by the comprehensive HDX-MS and functional assay data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Ligand-dependent conformational changes originate at the BSR and H3 interface.
source: The results presented here suggest that the ligand-dependent conformational changes originate at the BSR and H3 interface.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing that all modulators stabilize these regions and that stability of H3 and BSR correlates with overall receptor stability.

claim: SRC2 fusion to H12 mimics ligand-dependent stability around the distal orthosteric binding site including the BSR despite being 5 nm away.
source: Interestingly, SRC2 fusion to H12 mimics ligand-dependent stability around the distal orthosteric binding site including the BSR despite being 5 nm away.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data comparing the SRC2 fusion construct with liganded receptor.

claim: The SRC2 fusion construct used to solve the 'apo' crystal structure artificially locks RORγ in the active conformation.
source: Experiments reported here show that the SRC2 fusion construct used to solve the 'apo' crystal structure artificially locks RORγ in the active conformation.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data showing that the fusion construct exhibits similar dynamics to the ternary complex.

claim: A368V RORγLBD does not respond to endogenous ligand and has little to no intrinsic activity in promotor-reporter assays.
source: To address the ligand-dependent activity of RORγ, we employed a 'bump-and-hole' strategy where A368V RORγLBD does not respond to endogenous ligand and has little to no intrinsic activity in promotor-reporter assays.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data showing loss of function with the A368V mutation.

claim: Both WT and A368V RORγ show similar deuterium exchange kinetics suggesting similar conformational ensemble.
source: Regardless, both WT and A368V RORγ show similar deuterium exchange kinetics suggesting similar conformational ensemble, have little intrinsic activity in vitro, and are able to be activated by synthetic ligands that can bind the mutant construct.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data comparing WT and A368V variants.

claim: Endogenous ligands are required for the observed activity of RORγ in cells.
source: Taken together, these observations are collectively consistent with the model where endogenous ligands are required for the observed activity in cells.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the A368V mutation data showing loss of basal activity that is recoverable with synthetic ligands.

claim: Unliganded RORγ is likely a dynamic ensemble of conformations where H12 makes a disordered-to-ordered transition upon ligand binding.
source: Based on the two-step activation model, a more accurate depiction of unliganded RORγ is a dynamic ensemble of conformations where H12 makes a disordered-to-ordered transition upon ligand binding and is further stabilized with coactivator peptide binding.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS data showing H12 dynamics and the effects of ligand and coactivator binding.

claim: RORγ agonists must not only out compete endogenous ligands, but also stabilize a conformer that is more productive in driving association with coactivators than the endogenous agonists in order to hyperactivate the receptor.
source: According to this model, RORγ agonists must not only out compete endogenous ligands, but also stabilize a conformer that is more productive in driving association with coactivators than the endogenous agonists in order to hyperactivate the receptor.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the comprehensive structural and functional data showing that hyperactivating ligands enhance coactivator affinity beyond that of endogenous ligands.

claim: Modulators that activate RORγ to the same level as endogenous ligands should be considered silent agonists.
source: Modulators that activate RORγ to the same level should be considered silent agonists, Figure 6B.
evidence: The claim is a conceptual model proposed based on the experimental findings.

claim: HDX-MS measurements can distinguish agonists from inverse agonists.
source: These findings are consistent with previously observed pharmacology (Kumar et al., 2012) and show that HDX-MS measurements can distinguish agonists from inverse agonists.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data showing distinct protection patterns for agonists versus inverse agonists, corroborated by citation to Kumar et al., 2012.

claim: Hydrophobic interactions with BSR amino acids F378 and F388 help explain dramatic protections to deuterium exchange to the β-sheet region observed by HDX-MS.
source: Importantly, hydrophobic interactions observed by both compounds with BSR amino acids, F378 and F388, help explain dramatic protections to deuterium exchange to the β-sheet region (BSR) observed by HDX-MS.
evidence: The claim integrates X-ray crystallography data with HDX-MS observations.

claim: SR19265 and SR19355 co-crystal structures were solved with 2.7 and 2.3 Å resolution respectively.
source: Both SR19265 and SR19355 co-crystal structures were solved with 2.7 and 2.3 Å resolution respectively, Figure 1A-Supplementary file 1 and Figure 2A—figure supplement 1B-C.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data.

claim: SR19265 and SR19355 share similar binding poses within the ligand binding pocket and make general hydrophobic contacts through the indoline and substituted benzoyl moieties with H3, H7 and H10.
source: In general, SR19265 and SR19355 share similar binding poses within the ligand binding pocket and make general hydrophobic contacts through the indoline and substituted benzoyl moieties with H3, H7 and H10 where protection to HDX is also observed, Figure 2B and C.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography and HDX-MS data shown in Figures 2B and C.

claim: SR19355 treatment further reduces coactivator peptide interaction and robustly reduced RORγ activity in cells.
source: As expected, SR19355 treatment further reduces coactivator peptide interaction, and like SR2211, SR19355 also robustly reduced RORγ activity in cells, Figure 2F.
evidence: The claim is supported by functional assay data shown in Figure 2F.

claim: Compound performance in the AlphaScreen-based peptide recruitment assay correlated with affinity for coactivator peptide determined by fluorescence polarization.
source: Compound performance in the AlphaScreen-based peptide recruitment assay was found to correlate with affinity for coactivator peptide determined by fluorescence polarization, Figures 2E and 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1F.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of data from two different assay formats.

claim: The DMSO-treated receptor had a melt temperature of 45.0 °C in the thermal shift assay.
source: In the thermal shift assay, the DMSO-treated receptor had a melt temperature of 45.0 °C and compounds shifted the melt temperature (ΔTm) by 4.2–13.2 °C (median of 7.8 °C) in a distribution that appeared normal, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: The claim is supported by thermal shift assay data.

claim: Compounds shifted the melt temperature by 4.2–13.2 °C with a median of 7.8 °C.
source: In the thermal shift assay, the DMSO-treated receptor had a melt temperature of 45.0 °C and compounds shifted the melt temperature (ΔTm) by 4.2–13.2 °C (median of 7.8 °C) in a distribution that appeared normal, Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.
evidence: The claim is supported by thermal shift assay data.

claim: Compounds generally clustered into three groups based on H12 stabilization: those that did not stabilize H12, partial agonists that weakly stabilize H12, and those that strongly stabilized H12.
source: The collection of ligands showed a wide range of deuterium exchange protection within H12. Compounds generally clustered into three groups; the first included compounds that did not stabilize H12 (likely antagonists or inverse agonists), the second group consisted of partial agonists that weakly stabilize H12, and the constituents of the third group strongly stabilized H12.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS screening data of 38 compounds.

claim: Protection to deuterium exchange in H2, H3, H7, the BSR, and H10 correlated with coactivator peptide activity.
source: We also observed that perturbation values of H4 at the 4 hr timepoint correlated (R2 = 0.476) with coactivator recruitment activity, Figure 3B. Furthermore, protection to deuterium exchange in H2, H3, H7, the BSR, and H10 also correlated with coactivator peptide activity, Figure 3D.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of HDX-MS and functional assay data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: SR19355 displayed much higher performance in thermal stability assay with no commensurate increase in protection at regions that correlate with thermal stability.
source: Importantly, SR19355 displayed much higher performance in this assay with no commensurate increase in protection at these regions. This highlights an important limitation to the approach where differences in binding mode (an additional hydrogen bond in this case) can identify compounds as outliers.
evidence: The claim is supported by comparison of thermal shift and HDX-MS data.

claim: Perturbation values of peptides from H2, H3, the BSR, H7, and H12 were found to have significantly non-zero correlation coefficients with cell-based activity.
source: Perturbation values of peptides originating in H2, H3, the BSR, H7, and H12 were found to have significantly non-zero correlation coefficients, Figure 3J.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis of HDX-MS and cell-based assay data shown in Figure 3J.

claim: Perturbation values of a peptide from H2 correlated strongly with peptides from the BSR (R2 = 0.698).
source: Perturbation values of this peptide correlated strongly peptides from the BSR (R2 = 0.698), Figure 4H.
evidence: The claim is supported by covariation analysis of HDX-MS data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: K354 and K503 form several hydrogen bonds with backbone carbonyl groups.
source: RORγ in the active conformation (PDB ID 3L0L) reveals that K354 and K503 form several hydrogen bonds with backbone carbonyl shown in red.
evidence: The claim is supported by X-ray crystallography data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: General electrostatic interactions at K503 but not K354 are sufficient for activation.
source: Mutation to K503R, but not K354R, was able to retain activity similar to WT levels, indicating general electrostatic interactions at K503 but not K354 are sufficient for activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis data showing that arginine substitution at K503 retains activity but not at K354.

claim: The H12-H4 interaction is essential to activate RORγ in situ.
source: Treatment with synthetic agonist SR19547 was able to recover activity of the K503A construct, but not the K354A mutant suggesting the H12-H4 interaction is essential to activate RORγ in situ.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis and functional assay data.

claim: Intramolecular K503 interaction is only required for activation by endogenous ligands.
source: Treatment with synthetic agonist SR19265 was able to recover some activity of the K503A construct and K354A at high concentrations suggesting the interaction between H12 and H4 is essential to activate RORγ in situ, while intramolecular K503 interaction is only required for activation by endogenous ligands.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis and functional assay data showing differential recovery with synthetic versus endogenous ligands.

claim: Comparing WT RORγLBD + SR19265 to K354A RORγLBD + SR19265 reveals no significant differences in deuterium exchange to peptides surrounding the orthosteric binding pocket.
source: Comparing WT RORγLBD + SR19265 to K354A RORγLBD + SR19265 reveals no significant differences in deuterium exchange to peptides surrounding the orthosteric binding pocket. Specifically, the exchange signature of the BSR was identical across all three constructs indicating ligand binding, Figure 5I.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS data shown in Figure 5I.

claim: The mutagenesis studies suggest decoupling of ligand-binding from ligand mediated activation.
source: Taken together, these observations suggest decoupling of ligand-binding from ligand mediated activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from HDX-MS and functional data showing that K354A binds ligand but does not activate.

claim: The disparity between activation of RORγ in vitro and in cells was evident by the strength of the correlations for different regions of the protein.
source: The disparity between activation of RORγ in vitro and in cells was evident by the strength of the correlations for different regions of the protein.
evidence: The claim is supported by statistical analysis showing different correlation patterns for in vitro versus cell-based assays.

claim: Stability of H2 is likely a general indicator of global stability and activation potential.
source: This is likely due to several biochemical activities required to hyperactivate the receptor in cellulo. As H2 stability generally correlated with H3, the BSR, H7 and H12, it is likely that stability of this region of the protein could serve as general indicator of global stability and activation potential.
evidence: The claim is inferred from correlation analysis showing H2 stability correlates with multiple regions and with cell-based activity.

claim: Every modulator stabilized the BSR and H3 regions.
source: Not only did every modulator stabilize these regions, but the stability of H3 and the BSR correlated with ligand-dependent stability of the receptor.
evidence: The claim is supported by HDX-MS screening data of 38 compounds.

claim: The use of mutagenesis to selectively disrupt H10-12, but not the orthosteric binding site suggests that several intramolecular interactions are required to stabilize AF2.
source: In addition, the use of mutagenesis to selectively disrupt H10-12, but not the orthosteric binding site suggests that several intramolecular interactions are required to stabilize AF2.
evidence: The claim is inferred from mutagenesis data showing that K354A and K503A disrupt H10-12 stability without affecting ligand binding.

claim: RORγ is able to bind a coactivator peptide with excessive amounts of protein in vitro, but this low affinity interaction is likely not biologically relevant.
source: While RORγ is able to bind a coactivator peptide with excessive amounts of protein in vitro, this low affinity interaction is likely not biologically relevant.
evidence: The claim is inferred from functional assay data showing weak coactivator binding in the absence of ligand.

claim: An important limitation to the A368V strategy is that the mutation may disrupt both the binding and activation by endogenous ligands but also the structure of the 'apo' protein responsible for the intrinsic constitutive activity.
